# Learning Log — Breaking Down a User Story (PDP Product Information Accordion) as FED Lead

**Date:** 2026-08-07
**Context:** Jasmijn (BA) owns `SFCC-195` — the PDP "Product Information Accordion" (the expandable tabs: Details & Care, Size & Fit, Shipping & Returns, Assistance, plus an EU-only Environmental Qualities). Tim has been pushing the team to write smaller, "component-based" user stories rather than one monolith. Jas asked for my thoughts on how to split it. Her first cut was **shell + one story per tab = 6 stories**. Over a couple of exchanges we landed on a data-source-based split, and resolved a specific question about whether the Assistance tab deserved its own story.
**Role lens:** Front-End Development Lead (spans both squads). I'm Claude-assisted, so this log is where I make the reasoning *mine* rather than just shipping the reply I sent Jas.

---

## 0. Why this log exists

The disposable part is the exact answer for `SFCC-195` (4 stories vs 6, Assistance bundled with Shipping & Returns). The **reusable** part is:

1. **The heuristic** — how I decide where a UI story should be *cut*.
2. **The pattern-recognition** — spotting that the team *already* has a component-based story convention, and citing its precedent instead of inventing one.
3. **The dependency discipline** — how I stop a later-sprint / other-squad integration from silently getting pulled into a current story.
4. **The stakeholder register** — how I give a BA advice that lands, and counter-propose without steamrolling.

Those transfer to every backlog-refinement conversation. The specific accordion split does not.

---

## 1. Lesson: slice a story by its *seam*, not by its *surface*

Jas's instinct was to slice by what the user sees — one tab, one story. That's the intuitive cut, and it's wrong for the same reason "one story per button" would be: **the UI surface is not where the work or the risk lives.**

When I mapped each tab to *where its content actually comes from*, the real structure appeared:

| Tab | Data source | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Details & Care | SFCC product attribute | HTML → sanitize → render |
| Size & Fit | SFCC (+ optional Contentful fallback) | same path; needs a *new* attribute (unconfirmed) |
| Shipping & Returns | Contentful (region-keyed) | rich-text render |
| Assistance | Contentful (region-keyed) + **1 special control** | same as S&R *except* "Start a Chat" |
| Environmental Qualities | **AP21**, EU-only, render-only-if-present | different source + regional gating |

Four of the five are structurally identical (a title + an expandable rich-text panel). Splitting per-tab produces near-clone stories that differ only by which content key they read — that's config, not a story's worth of build + QA. Worse, a "shell with nothing in it" story is a **horizontal slice**: it can't satisfy an acceptance criterion a PO can read ("shopper can see X"), so it's only "done" on faith.

**Takeaway:** a story should be a **vertical slice** — thin, but end-to-end and demoable. Cut along the seam where the build effort, the data path, and the risk actually change (here: the data source), not along the visual boundary. My recommended cut was ~4 stories by data source, with the shell carrying the first real tab as a walking skeleton so it's demoable on its own.

---

## 2. Lesson: the "component-based" pattern is already in the backlog — recognise it and cite the precedent

Tim's direction sounds abstract until you notice the team has *already been doing it*. Two live examples I found and used as evidence:

- **Filters:** `SFCC-104` *Filters & Facets — BM Configuration (Shared)* → `SFCC-108` *Search Results – Filters & Facets **UI Component*** → `SFCC-199` *PLP UI – Filters & Facets Component*, whose description literally says *"a shared filter panel component like in SFCC-108… scopes the integration of that component into the PLP page template."*
- **Recently Viewed:** `SFCC-83` *Recently Viewed UI Component (Shared)* — *"built once and reused across multiple page contexts"* — and it **peeled its consent concern out** into `SFCC-106`.

So the house pattern is: **(shared enabler / config) → (reusable component) → (per-page integration), and lift cross-cutting concerns into their own story.** That's what "component-based" means *here*.

**Takeaway:** as a lead, my proposals are far stronger when they're framed as *"this is the same shape as SFCC-104/108/199"* than as a novel idea. Precedent lowers the cost of a yes, keeps the backlog internally consistent, and shows I've read the board. Before proposing a decomposition, go find the last time the team decomposed something similar.

---

## 3. Lesson: the real story boundaries are *data source + dependency + readiness* — a two-level cut

Slicing by data source is the first cut. The second cut is by **risk / readiness**, and it's why I split two same-source tabs apart:

- **Details & Care** and **Size & Fit** are both SFCC — same data path. By my own rule they'd be one story. But Size & Fit needs a *new* "model size" product attribute that's still unconfirmed with the business (flagged in `SFCC-89`'s comments, "to discuss with Dani"). So I put Details & Care in the shell (lowest risk, uses existing copy) and isolated Size & Fit — so the shell isn't held hostage to an open data question.

**Takeaway:** don't slice on data source alone. Ask *"does this part carry a different unknown — an unconfirmed attribute, an unbuilt integration, content that isn't authored yet?"* Where the readiness differs, split, so a ready slice can ship without waiting on a not-ready one. Same-source is a reason to group; different-risk is a reason to separate.

---

## 4. Lesson: never drag a later-sprint / other-squad integration into a current story — degrade instead

This was the crux of the Assistance question. Jas asked: *does Assistance have "more logic" than Shipping & Returns?* The design shows email, phone, hours, WhatsApp, a Contact Us link (external Zendesk redirect per PRD-022) — and a **"Start a Chat"** control.

Everything except Start a Chat is region-keyed Contentful text/links — identical in shape to Shipping & Returns. The one genuinely different thing is Start a Chat, and when I checked `.docs/integration/14-inside-chat.md` + `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md`, the important facts were:

- Inside Chat (Powerfront) loads as a **direct head tag, async, post-Didomi-consent**; the widget **owns its own availability** ("not shown when agents offline" is *its* rule, not ours to build).
- It's **Squad B, Sprint 7** work — a different squad, a later sprint. It does not exist in the build yet, and its site token + Didomi category are still open items.

`AGENTS.md` Hard Rule #14 is explicit: *never reference code from a later sprint; check `sprintScope.md` first.* So bundling "launch the consent-gated chat widget with live availability" into a Sprint 2/3 PDP story would pull a Sprint 7 integration forward — exactly the anti-pattern the rule guards against.

The resolution — and the transferable move — was **graceful degradation as a scoping lever**: build the accordion (and the chat control) now, rendering the control degrade-safe (if the widget's loaded it opens it, otherwise it does nothing); wire the actual launch when Inside Chat lands. Jas kept Assistance + Shipping & Returns as **one** story, and the chat trigger becomes a small deferred dependency logged against the Sprint 7 work. Build unblocked, nothing lost.

**Takeaway:** when a piece of a story touches an integration owned elsewhere or scheduled later, don't split the *content* around it and don't pull it forward — carve out the *behaviour* as a deferred dependency and design the current build to degrade gracefully until it lands. "Renders now, wired later" keeps the story whole and the build moving. This is the same move `SFCC-83` made peeling consent into `SFCC-106`.

---

## 5. Lesson: guard doc integrity — a ticket must not quietly settle an open PRD question

`SFCC-195`'s description asserts a content-ownership mapping (Details & Care + Size & Fit = SFCC; the rest = Contentful). But `.docs/prd/pdp.md` §18 still lists *"Product copy ownership (Contentful vs SFCC vs AP21) — TBD"* as an open item, and `.docs/integration/02-contentful.md` says PDP block ownership is pending. Per `AGENTS.md`'s doc-integrity rule, a ticket shouldn't silently pre-empt an unresolved PRD item — because the whole decomposition is *built on* that mapping.

**Takeaway:** before I let a split depend on a "fact," I check it against the source-of-truth doc. If the ticket is ahead of the PRD, I surface it ("just confirm this is signed off") rather than build on an assumption. A decomposition founded on an unconfirmed premise re-opens the moment the premise moves.

---

## 6. Lesson: advise a BA in *their* register — scope and dependencies, not rendering internals

My internal reasoning was full of dev detail (sanitize, degrade-safe control, consent-gated loader, walking skeleton). The reply that actually landed with Jas translated all of that into **her** currency: story count, what's bundled, what's a dependency, which sprint/squad owns it, and what unblocks the build. I also:

- **Conceded where her approach wins** (per-tab gives finer tracking + parallel pickup + per-tab content readiness) instead of only defending mine — so it read as a joint decision, not a takedown.
- **Reframed the disagreement as narrow** — it's "story vs sub-task granularity," which is cheap to adjust — so we could converge fast.

This mirrors the register lesson from my motion-review log: **the analysis and the communication are two separate deliverables.** Do the deep one for myself (and this log); send the compressed, audience-shaped one.

**Takeaway:** the fastest way to get a BA to "yes" is to speak in scope, dependency, and sprint terms, concede the real trade-offs, and shrink the disagreement to something adjustable.

---

## 7. Project knowledge captured (facts worth keeping)

- **PDP is not overridden yet.** The PDP still runs entirely from the base template; there is no `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/`. The base ships a hardcoded 4-item accordion partial (`information-accordion.jsx`: Product Detail / Size & Fit / Reviews / Questions) that **does not match our tab set** — the shell story is a copy-first override that replaces it with a data-driven Zimmermann component (`Commerce/` in Storybook).
- **Coordination hazard:** `SFCC-89` (Static Product Info) and `SFCC-92` (Size Selector) are both mine and both touch the not-yet-existing PDP override. Whoever overrides `product-detail/` first sets the structure — agree that up front.
- **Contentful pattern already exists:** `overrides/app/hooks/useContentful.ts`, `overrides/app/config/contentful.ts`, and `overrides/app/components/contentful/productHero.tsx` — which encodes the ownership rule *Contentful references the product id; SFCC owns the attributes.* New Contentful-sourced tabs plug into this; they depend on the content model from `SFCC-249` (still in review).
- **Tab → source map** (see table in §1) is the backbone of the whole split.
- **Size Guide is NOT an accordion tab** — it's a separate Measmerize slide-out with a Contentful fallback (`pdp.md` §11, story `SFCC-102`). Don't conflate it with Size & Fit.
- **Environmental Qualities** is EU-only (`/en-eu/`, `/fr-eu/`), sourced from AP21, renders only when data exists (PRD-009) — genuinely its own story.
- **Inside Chat** = Powerfront, head-tag + post-consent, widget owns its own visibility, Squad B / Sprint 7, open items on token + Didomi category.

---

## 8. Reusable checklist — "Breaking down a UI user story" (keep this)

1. **Read the whole context first:** the ticket, the PRD section(s) it cites, the matching `.docs/integration/NN-*.md`, `sprintScope.md`, and the actual code state in `overrides/` (does the thing even exist yet?).
2. **Map each sub-element to its data source** (SFCC / Contentful / AP21 / other) and its **dependencies** (which integration, which config, which other ticket).
3. **Group by data source** — that's the first cut.
4. **Split again where risk/readiness differs** — an unconfirmed attribute, unauthored content, an unbuilt integration.
5. **Make each story a vertical slice** — thin but demoable. Give an enabling/"shell" story a real first slice so it isn't a horizontal orphan.
6. **Quarantine later-sprint / other-squad work** (Hard Rule #14) — carve it out as a deferred dependency and design the current build to **degrade gracefully**; don't pull it forward, don't fragment the content around it.
7. **Cite the team's own precedent** (`SFCC-104/108/199`, `SFCC-83/106`) so the split matches the house pattern.
8. **Check the ticket against the source-of-truth doc** — flag anything the ticket assumes that the PRD still lists as open.
9. **Offer sub-tasks, not more stories,** when a stakeholder wants finer granularity — keeps their visibility without orphan/duplicate stories.
10. **Write the reply in the stakeholder's register** — scope, dependencies, sprints; concede the trade-offs; shrink the disagreement.

---

## 9. Open threads / next steps for me

- **Log the chat-trigger dependency** so "set up later" doesn't evaporate — an AC line on the story *and/or* a small follow-up linked to the Sprint 7 Inside Chat work: *"Start a Chat renders from Contentful but is not wired to the widget until Inside Chat lands (Sprint 7)."* Protects QA from logging it as a bug and reminds whoever builds Inside Chat to circle back.
- **Chase the content-ownership sign-off** (Contentful vs SFCC vs AP21) before these stories are written up — the split depends on it. Specifically confirm whether Assistance is Contentful editorial or just static links.
- **Confirm the Size & Fit "model size" attribute** with the business (the Dani thread on `SFCC-89`) — it gates that story.
- **Agree the PDP-override ownership** with myself across `SFCC-89` / `SFCC-92` / the accordion shell so we don't override `product-detail/` twice in parallel.

---

*Source material for this log: `SFCC-195` and its neighbours (`SFCC-89`, `SFCC-92`, `SFCC-26`, `SFCC-102`, `SFCC-108`, `SFCC-199`, `SFCC-104`, `SFCC-83`, `SFCC-106`, `SFCC-249`), mapped against `AGENTS.md` (Hard Rule #14, doc-integrity), `.docs/prd/pdp.md`, `.docs/integration/14-inside-chat.md`, `.docs/integration/02-contentful.md`, `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md`, and the base-vs-overrides PDP code state, on 2026-08-07.*

Tim's direction sounds abstract until you notice the team has *already been doing it*. Two live examples I found and used as evidence:

- **Filters:** `SFCC-104` *Filters & Facets — BM Configuration (Shared)* → `SFCC-108` *Search Results – Filters & Facets **UI Component*** → `SFCC-199` *PLP UI – Filters & Facets Component*, whose description literally says *"a shared filter panel component like in SFCC-108… scopes the integration of that component into the PLP page template."*
- **Recently Viewed:** `SFCC-83` *Recently Viewed UI Component (Shared)* — *"built once and reused across multiple page contexts"* — and it **peeled its consent concern out** into `SFCC-106`.

So the house pattern is: **(shared enabler / config) → (reusable component) → (per-page integration), and lift cross-cutting concerns into their own story.** That's what "component-based" means *here*.

**Takeaway:** as a lead, my proposals are far stronger when they're framed as *"this is the same shape as SFCC-104/108/199"* than as a novel idea. Precedent lowers the cost of a yes, keeps the backlog internally consistent, and shows I've read the board. Before proposing a decomposition, go find the last time the team decomposed something similar.

---

## 3. Lesson: the real story boundaries are *data source + dependency + readiness* — a two-level cut

Slicing by data source is the first cut. The second cut is by **risk / readiness**, and it's why I split two same-source tabs apart:

- **Details & Care** and **Size & Fit** are both SFCC — same data path. By my own rule they'd be one story. But Size & Fit needs a *new* "model size" product attribute that's still unconfirmed with the business (flagged in `SFCC-89`'s comments, "to discuss with Dani"). So I put Details & Care in the shell (lowest risk, uses existing copy) and isolated Size & Fit — so the shell isn't held hostage to an open data question.

**Takeaway:** don't slice on data source alone. Ask *"does this part carry a different unknown — an unconfirmed attribute, an unbuilt integration, content that isn't authored yet?"* Where the readiness differs, split, so a ready slice can ship without waiting on a not-ready one. Same-source is a reason to group; different-risk is a reason to separate.

---

## 4. Lesson: never drag a later-sprint / other-squad integration into a current story — degrade instead

This was the crux of the Assistance question. Jas asked: *does Assistance have "more logic" than Shipping & Returns?* The design shows email, phone, hours, WhatsApp, a Contact Us link (external Zendesk redirect per PRD-022) — and a **"Start a Chat"** control.

Everything except Start a Chat is region-keyed Contentful text/links — identical in shape to Shipping & Returns. The one genuinely different thing is Start a Chat, and when I checked `.docs/integration/14-inside-chat.md` + `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md`, the important facts were:

- Inside Chat (Powerfront) loads as a **direct head tag, async, post-Didomi-consent**; the widget **owns its own availability** ("not shown when agents offline" is *its* rule, not ours to build).
- It's **Squad B, Sprint 7** work — a different squad, a later sprint. It does not exist in the build yet, and its site token + Didomi category are still open items.

`AGENTS.md` Hard Rule #14 is explicit: *never reference code from a later sprint; check `sprintScope.md` first.* So bundling "launch the consent-gated chat widget with live availability" into a Sprint 2/3 PDP story would pull a Sprint 7 integration forward — exactly the anti-pattern the rule guards against.

The resolution — and the transferable move — was **graceful degradation as a scoping lever**: build the accordion (and the chat control) now, rendering the control degrade-safe (if the widget's loaded it opens it, otherwise it does nothing); wire the actual launch when Inside Chat lands. Jas kept Assistance + Shipping & Returns as **one** story, and the chat trigger becomes a small deferred dependency logged against the Sprint 7 work. Build unblocked, nothing lost.

**Takeaway:** when a piece of a story touches an integration owned elsewhere or scheduled later, don't split the *content* around it and don't pull it forward — carve out the *behaviour* as a deferred dependency and design the current build to degrade gracefully until it lands. "Renders now, wired later" keeps the story whole and the build moving. This is the same move `SFCC-83` made peeling consent into `SFCC-106`.

---

## 5. Lesson: guard doc integrity — a ticket must not quietly settle an open PRD question

`SFCC-195`'s description asserts a content-ownership mapping (Details & Care + Size & Fit = SFCC; the rest = Contentful). But `.docs/prd/pdp.md` §18 still lists *"Product copy ownership (Contentful vs SFCC vs AP21) — TBD"* as an open item, and `.docs/integration/02-contentful.md` says PDP block ownership is pending. Per `AGENTS.md`'s doc-integrity rule, a ticket shouldn't silently pre-empt an unresolved PRD item — because the whole decomposition is *built on* that mapping.

**Takeaway:** before I let a split depend on a "fact," I check it against the source-of-truth doc. If the ticket is ahead of the PRD, I surface it ("just confirm this is signed off") rather than build on an assumption. A decomposition founded on an unconfirmed premise re-opens the moment the premise moves.

---

## 6. Lesson: advise a BA in *their* register — scope and dependencies, not rendering internals

My internal reasoning was full of dev detail (sanitize, degrade-safe control, consent-gated loader, walking skeleton). The reply that actually landed with Jas translated all of that into **her** currency: story count, what's bundled, what's a dependency, which sprint/squad owns it, and what unblocks the build. I also:

- **Conceded where her approach wins** (per-tab gives finer tracking + parallel pickup + per-tab content readiness) instead of only defending mine — so it read as a joint decision, not a takedown.
- **Reframed the disagreement as narrow** — it's "story vs sub-task granularity," which is cheap to adjust — so we could converge fast.

This mirrors the register lesson from my motion-review log: **the analysis and the communication are two separate deliverables.** Do the deep one for myself (and this log); send the compressed, audience-shaped one.

**Takeaway:** the fastest way to get a BA to "yes" is to speak in scope, dependency, and sprint terms, concede the real trade-offs, and shrink the disagreement to something adjustable.

---

## 7. Project knowledge captured (facts worth keeping)

- **PDP is not overridden yet.** The PDP still runs entirely from the base template; there is no `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/`. The base ships a hardcoded 4-item accordion partial (`information-accordion.jsx`: Product Detail / Size & Fit / Reviews / Questions) that **does not match our tab set** — the shell story is a copy-first override that replaces it with a data-driven Zimmermann component (`Commerce/` in Storybook).
- **Coordination hazard:** `SFCC-89` (Static Product Info) and `SFCC-92` (Size Selector) are both mine and both touch the not-yet-existing PDP override. Whoever overrides `product-detail/` first sets the structure — agree that up front.
- **Contentful pattern already exists:** `overrides/app/hooks/useContentful.ts`, `overrides/app/config/contentful.ts`, and `overrides/app/components/contentful/productHero.tsx` — which encodes the ownership rule *Contentful references the product id; SFCC owns the attributes.* New Contentful-sourced tabs plug into this; they depend on the content model from `SFCC-249` (still in review).
- **Tab → source map** (see table in §1) is the backbone of the whole split.
- **Size Guide is NOT an accordion tab** — it's a separate Measmerize slide-out with a Contentful fallback (`pdp.md` §11, story `SFCC-102`). Don't conflate it with Size & Fit.
- **Environmental Qualities** is EU-only (`/en-eu/`, `/fr-eu/`), sourced from AP21, renders only when data exists (PRD-009) — genuinely its own story.
- **Inside Chat** = Powerfront, head-tag + post-consent, widget owns its own visibility, Squad B / Sprint 7, open items on token + Didomi category.

---

## 8. Reusable checklist — "Breaking down a UI user story" (keep this)

1. **Read the whole context first:** the ticket, the PRD section(s) it cites, the matching `.docs/integration/NN-*.md`, `sprintScope.md`, and the actual code state in `overrides/` (does the thing even exist yet?).
2. **Map each sub-element to its data source** (SFCC / Contentful / AP21 / other) and its **dependencies** (which integration, which config, which other ticket).
3. **Group by data source** — that's the first cut.
4. **Split again where risk/readiness differs** — an unconfirmed attribute, unauthored content, an unbuilt integration.
5. **Make each story a vertical slice** — thin but demoable. Give an enabling/"shell" story a real first slice so it isn't a horizontal orphan.
6. **Quarantine later-sprint / other-squad work** (Hard Rule #14) — carve it out as a deferred dependency and design the current build to **degrade gracefully**; don't pull it forward, don't fragment the content around it.
7. **Cite the team's own precedent** (`SFCC-104/108/199`, `SFCC-83/106`) so the split matches the house pattern.
8. **Check the ticket against the source-of-truth doc** — flag anything the ticket assumes that the PRD still lists as open.
9. **Offer sub-tasks, not more stories,** when a stakeholder wants finer granularity — keeps their visibility without orphan/duplicate stories.
10. **Write the reply in the stakeholder's register** — scope, dependencies, sprints; concede the trade-offs; shrink the disagreement.

---

## 9. Open threads / next steps for me

- **Log the chat-trigger dependency** so "set up later" doesn't evaporate — an AC line on the story *and/or* a small follow-up linked to the Sprint 7 Inside Chat work: *"Start a Chat renders from Contentful but is not wired to the widget until Inside Chat lands (Sprint 7)."* Protects QA from logging it as a bug and reminds whoever builds Inside Chat to circle back.

- **Confirm the Size & Fit "model size" attribute** with the business (the Dani thread on `SFCC-89`) — it gates that story.
- **Agree the PDP-override ownership** with myself across `SFCC-89` / `SFCC-92` / the accordion shell so we don't override `product-detail/` twice in parallel.

# Breaking a big user story into small ones — the plain-English version

> **Who this is for:** me (FED lead) — the clear, low-jargon version I can actually retain.
> **What it's from:** Jas (our BA) asked how to split `SFCC-195`, the PDP "Product Information
> Accordion" (those expandable tabs on the product page). Tim's been pushing everyone to write
> smaller, "one-component-at-a-time" stories. This is what I took away.
> **The deal:** simplified, not dumbed down. Where I use a real name (Contentful, AP21…), I explain
> it in normal words the first time. Glossary at the bottom.

---

## The one thing to really get

Picture the accordion as a **filing cabinet**, and each tab as a **drawer**:

> Details & Care · Size & Fit · Shipping & Returns · Assistance · Environmental Qualities

Jas's first idea: **one ticket per drawer.** Feels tidy.

Here's the catch — **all the drawers look the same** (a label, and some text that opens up). The thing that's actually *different* is **where the paper inside each drawer comes from**:

- **Details & Care, Size & Fit** → from the **product record** (info stored on the product itself)
- **Shipping & Returns, Assistance** → from **Contentful** (the tool the content team edits without a developer)
- **Environmental Qualities** → from **AP21** (the product data system), EU shops only

So the smart cut isn't "one ticket per drawer." It's **"group the drawers by where their paper comes from."**

➡️ **The lesson in one line: split by where the content comes from, not by what the shopper sees.**

Why? Because the real work is building the *pipe* that fetches each kind of paper. Two drawers fed by the same pipe = the same work = one ticket. Splitting them into two tickets just means building the same pipe twice.

That took Jas's 6 tickets down to about 4, cut along the pipes instead of the drawers.

---

## Lesson 1 — a ticket should be something you can actually show

Jas's plan started with a "just the empty cabinet, no drawers" ticket. Problem: **you can't demo an empty cabinet.** Nobody can look at it and go "yep, that works."

Fix: **put one real drawer inside the cabinet ticket** so there's something to see and tick off.

➡️ Rule of thumb: every ticket should be a thin but *whole* strip — something a person can look at and sign off — never a hidden layer no one can see.

---

## Lesson 2 — we've done this before, so copy the pattern (don't invent one)

When Tim says "component-based stories," he's describing something the team **already did** on the filters work:
- one ticket to build the shared piece once,
- one ticket to plug it into each page.

(For the record: `SFCC-108` built the shared filter component, `SFCC-199` plugged it into the listing page. "Recently Viewed," `SFCC-83`, did the same.)

➡️ Lesson for me as lead: my proposals get an easy "yes" when I say *"this is the same shape as the filters work"* instead of inventing a new approach. Point at the last time we did it.

---

## Lesson 3 — split again when one drawer is riskier than another

Details & Care and Size & Fit both come from the product record — so by my own rule, that's one ticket. **But** Size & Fit needs a **new bit of product info that doesn't exist yet** (someone still has to confirm it with the business). Details & Care uses info we already have.

So I kept them apart. If I bundle them, the safe one gets stuck waiting on the unsure one.

➡️ Rule of thumb: same source = group them. But if one piece is **waiting on an unknown** (info not confirmed, content not written, a tool not built) — split it off so it doesn't drag the rest down.

---

## Lesson 4 — don't drag in something another team is building later; let it wait politely

The "Assistance" drawer *looked* like it might be special. It has email, phone, opening hours, WhatsApp, a contact link… and a **"Start a Chat"** button.

Everything except the chat button is just text and links — same as the Shipping & Returns drawer. The chat button is the only real difference, because it opens the **live chat widget**, and that widget:
- can't switch on until the shopper accepts cookies,
- decides its own "are we online right now" behaviour,
- and is being built by **another team, in a later sprint** — it doesn't exist yet.

We have a written rule: **don't build against something from a later sprint.**

So the move was: **build the drawer now, but make the chat button harmless until the widget shows up.** If the chat's there, the button opens it; if not, it just sits quietly. Wire it up properly later, when the other team's part lands.

➡️ End result: Assistance stayed in **one** ticket with Shipping & Returns, and the chat button became a small "come back to this later" note tied to the other team's work. Nothing got blocked.

(The proper name for "still works, just quietly does less, when a piece is missing" is *graceful degradation*. Worth knowing — it's often the trick that lets you keep one ticket instead of splitting or blocking.)

---

## Lesson 5 — if the ticket assumes something the spec hasn't decided, say so

The ticket confidently said "these drawers come from Contentful, those from the product record." But our actual spec (the PRD) **still lists that exact decision as "not decided yet."**

I flagged it — politely — because the whole split leans on that decision. If it changes later, the split falls apart.

➡️ Lesson: before I build a plan on a "fact," I check the spec. If the ticket is running ahead of the spec, I raise it instead of quietly assuming.

---

## Lesson 6 — talk to a BA in BA language

In my head this was all "fetch, sanitise, cookie-gate, degrade." What I actually **sent Jas** was: how many tickets, what's bundled, what's a dependency, which team/sprint owns what, and what keeps us unblocked.

I also said out loud where **her** idea was better (more tickets = easier to track progress and hand out to different people), so it felt like we decided together — not like I overruled her.

➡️ Lesson: do the deep thinking for myself; send the plain, scope-and-dependencies version to them. And always name the trade-offs of their idea — it builds trust and gets to "yes" faster.

---

## My quick checklist (steal this next time)

1. **Read everything first** — the ticket, the spec bit it points to, and check whether the thing even exists in our code yet.
2. For each part, ask **"where does its content come from?"** and group the parts that share a source.
3. **Split again** wherever one part is waiting on an unknown.
4. Make every ticket **demoable** — give the "shell" ticket one real drawer.
5. Anything **another team / later sprint owns** → don't pull it in; build it to sit quietly until their part lands.
6. **Point at the last time we split something the same way** — makes the "yes" easy.
7. If the ticket assumes something the spec hasn't settled, **flag it.**
8. Someone wants more tickets just for tracking? Use **sub-tasks**, not extra stories.
9. Write the reply in **their** language, and name where their idea wins.

---

## Words I used (so they stop being scary)

- **Vertical slice / walking skeleton** — a thin but *complete* piece you can actually show and tick off. Opposite: an invisible layer no one can see.
- **Data source** — where a piece of content actually comes from (our product system vs the content tool vs AP21).
- **Dependency** — something this work needs that lives elsewhere (another ticket, team, or sprint).
- **Graceful degradation** — building it so it still works, just quietly does less, when a piece it wants isn't ready yet.
- **Cookie-gated / consent-gated** — can't switch on until the shopper accepts cookies.
- **Contentful** — the content tool the marketing/content team edits without needing a developer.
- **AP21** — the product data system a lot of our product info comes from.
- **PRD** — the spec / "what we agreed to build" document. Source of truth for requirements.
- **Sprint / squad** — a sprint is a ~2-week chunk of work; a squad is one of our two teams. "Later sprint / other squad" = not our job right now.
- **Sub-task vs story** — a story is a standalone chunk of value; a sub-task is a checklist item *inside* a story. Use sub-tasks when you want finer tracking without more standalone tickets.

---

## Still to do
- Write the "chat button hooks up later" note somewhere it won't get lost (on the ticket + linked to the chat-widget work).
- Chase the "where does the content come from" decision so it's actually confirmed.
- Confirm the new Size & Fit product info with the business.
- Make sure I don't end up building the product-page structure twice across my own tickets.

---

Jas's plan started with a "just the empty cabinet, no drawers" ticket. Problem: **you can't demo an empty cabinet.** Nobody can look at it and go "yep, that works."

Fix: **put one real drawer inside the cabinet ticket** so there's something to see and tick off.

➡️ Rule of thumb: every ticket should be a thin but *whole* strip — something a person can look at and sign off — never a hidden layer no one can see.

---

## Lesson 2 — we've done this before, so copy the pattern (don't invent one)

When Tim says "component-based stories," he's describing something the team **already did** on the filters work:
- one ticket to build the shared piece once,
- one ticket to plug it into each page.

(For the record: `SFCC-108` built the shared filter component, `SFCC-199` plugged it into the listing page. "Recently Viewed," `SFCC-83`, did the same.)

➡️ Lesson for me as lead: my proposals get an easy "yes" when I say *"this is the same shape as the filters work"* instead of inventing a new approach. Point at the last time we did it.

---

## Lesson 3 — split again when one drawer is riskier than another

Details & Care and Size & Fit both come from the product record — so by my own rule, that's one ticket. **But** Size & Fit needs a **new bit of product info that doesn't exist yet** (someone still has to confirm it with the business). Details & Care uses info we already have.

So I kept them apart. If I bundle them, the safe one gets stuck waiting on the unsure one.

➡️ Rule of thumb: same source = group them. But if one piece is **waiting on an unknown** (info not confirmed, content not written, a tool not built) — split it off so it doesn't drag the rest down.

---

## Lesson 4 — don't drag in something another team is building later; let it wait politely

The "Assistance" drawer *looked* like it might be special. It has email, phone, opening hours, WhatsApp, a contact link… and a **"Start a Chat"** button.

Everything except the chat button is just text and links — same as the Shipping & Returns drawer. The chat button is the only real difference, because it opens the **live chat widget**, and that widget:
- can't switch on until the shopper accepts cookies,
- decides its own "are we online right now" behaviour,
- and is being built by **another team, in a later sprint** — it doesn't exist yet.

We have a written rule: **don't build against something from a later sprint.**

So the move was: **build the drawer now, but make the chat button harmless until the widget shows up.** If the chat's there, the button opens it; if not, it just sits quietly. Wire it up properly later, when the other team's part lands.

➡️ End result: Assistance stayed in **one** ticket with Shipping & Returns, and the chat button became a small "come back to this later" note tied to the other team's work. Nothing got blocked.

(The proper name for "still works, just quietly does less, when a piece is missing" is *graceful degradation*. Worth knowing — it's often the trick that lets you keep one ticket instead of splitting or blocking.)

---

## Lesson 5 — if the ticket assumes something the spec hasn't decided, say so

The ticket confidently said "these drawers come from Contentful, those from the product record." But our actual spec (the PRD) **still lists that exact decision as "not decided yet."**

I flagged it — politely — because the whole split leans on that decision. If it changes later, the split falls apart.

➡️ Lesson: before I build a plan on a "fact," I check the spec. If the ticket is running ahead of the spec, I raise it instead of quietly assuming.

---

## Lesson 6 — talk to a BA in BA language

In my head this was all "fetch, sanitise, cookie-gate, degrade." What I actually **sent Jas** was: how many tickets, what's bundled, what's a dependency, which team/sprint owns what, and what keeps us unblocked.

I also said out loud where **her** idea was better (more tickets = easier to track progress and hand out to different people), so it felt like we decided together — not like I overruled her.

➡️ Lesson: do the deep thinking for myself; send the plain, scope-and-dependencies version to them. And always name the trade-offs of their idea — it builds trust and gets to "yes" faster.

---

## My quick checklist (steal this next time)

1. **Read everything first** — the ticket, the spec bit it points to, and check whether the thing even exists in our code yet.
2. For each part, ask **"where does its content come from?"** and group the parts that share a source.
3. **Split again** wherever one part is waiting on an unknown.
4. Make every ticket **demoable** — give the "shell" ticket one real drawer.
5. Anything **another team / later sprint owns** → don't pull it in; build it to sit quietly until their part lands.
6. **Point at the last time we split something the same way** — makes the "yes" easy.
7. If the ticket assumes something the spec hasn't settled, **flag it.**
8. Someone wants more tickets just for tracking? Use **sub-tasks**, not extra stories.
9. Write the reply in **their** language, and name where their idea wins.

---

## Words I used (so they stop being scary)

- **Vertical slice / walking skeleton** — a thin but *complete* piece you can actually show and tick off. Opposite: an invisible layer no one can see.
- **Data source** — where a piece of content actually comes from (our product system vs the content tool vs AP21).
- **Dependency** — something this work needs that lives elsewhere (another ticket, team, or sprint).
- **Graceful degradation** — building it so it still works, just quietly does less, when a piece it wants isn't ready yet.
- **Cookie-gated / consent-gated** — can't switch on until the shopper accepts cookies.
- **Contentful** — the content tool the marketing/content team edits without needing a developer.
- **AP21** — the product data system a lot of our product info comes from.
- **PRD** — the spec / "what we agreed to build" document. Source of truth for requirements.
- **Sprint / squad** — a sprint is a ~2-week chunk of work; a squad is one of our two teams. "Later sprint / other squad" = not our job right now.
- **Sub-task vs story** — a story is a standalone chunk of value; a sub-task is a checklist item *inside* a story. Use sub-tasks when you want finer tracking without more standalone tickets.
